{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nc-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"da32abab2995d72d58508602972b90c8b05c863cd74a34b7b4697744e0233dfa","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nc-class-c:lineage:32","source_registry_sha256":"e128656a3d00ba5437556728ebd87f5842c83601163739613417fe77cf9f423b","source_liveness_sha256":"dbfdf3e6d892a41c42c05809a9213d44a78aedd480dc6de23937c97292428b74"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Lane position, speed, curves, turning and following","heading":"C — Funeral processions, keeping right, speed for conditions, speed limits, curves, turning, following distance and lane changes (North Carolina)","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Funeral processions, keeping right, speed for conditions, speed limits, curves, turning, following distance and lane changes (North Carolina)
Knowledge domain: how to treat funeral processions and slow farm machinery, where to position your car, how speed changes stopping distance, the default North Carolina speed limits, and safe technique for curves, turns, following and lane changes.

FACT_ID: sec08-F01 | anchor: A01
Because farm equipment moves so slowly, the gap closes much faster than you expect as you come up behind it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F02 | anchor: A01
Farm equipment is allowed by law on most North Carolina roads, but not on interstates. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F03 | anchor: A01
Every vehicle in a funeral procession must drive with headlights on, and with hazard flashers on as well if it has them. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F04 | anchor: A01
The lead vehicle of a procession obeys all signals, but once it has crossed lawfully, or when an officer or funeral director directs it, or a police vehicle leads, the rest may go through the intersection without stopping, using extra care. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F05 | anchor: A01
Procession vehicles keep to the right side of the road and follow the car ahead as closely as is reasonable and prudent. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F06 | anchor: A01
An oncoming driver may choose to yield to a procession, and if so must either slow down or stop fully off the roadway so other oncoming traffic can stay in its lane. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F07 | anchor: A01
A driver going the same way as a procession must not pass it, unless the road is marked with two or more lanes moving in the procession's direction. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F08 | anchor: A01
Never knowingly drive between vehicles in a procession, and when it goes through a red light, do not enter the intersection on your green unless you can do so safely without crossing its path. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F09 | anchor: A01
The law requires driving on the right side of the road; the left side is legal only in cases such as one-way streets and passing. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F10 | anchor: A01
On a multi-lane highway, if you are going slower than the posted limit, use the far right lane except when passing, turning left or avoiding an obstruction. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F11 | anchor: A01
Your speed and your reaction time together set your stopping distance, and higher speed lengthens both the distance covered while reacting and the braking distance. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0054]

FACT_ID: sec08-F12 | anchor: A02
Even in ideal conditions a vehicle going 55 miles per hour needs about 211 feet to come to a complete stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F13 | anchor: A02
Every extra mile per hour reduces your control of the vehicle, and higher speed raises the chance that a crash will cause serious injury or death. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F14 | anchor: A02
Driving well below the limit is also dangerous; if you must go slowly, still keep to any posted minimum speed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F15 | anchor: A02
Very slow driving is especially risky just over the top of a hill or around a curve, where faster traffic may hit you before it can slow down. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F16 | anchor: A02
If a line of traffic builds behind you, it is wise to pull to the side, stop and let the vehicles go by. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F17 | anchor: A02
Never go faster than the posted limit, or faster than is reasonable and wise for the conditions at the time. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F18 | anchor: A02
The faster you travel, the farther ahead you need to see so that you have room to stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F19 | anchor: A02
Unless a sign says otherwise, the speed limit in cities and towns is 35 mph. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F20 | anchor: A02
The maximum speed is 45 mph for school buses and 55 mph for school activity buses. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F21 | anchor: A02
The maximum speed is 55 mph outside cities and towns and 70 mph on interstates. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F22 | anchor: A02
The handbook cites studies finding that a vehicle going well under the posted limit is far more likely to cause or be in a crash than one moving at normal speed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F23 | anchor: A02
Safe driving often means going slower than the posted limit, but never faster. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F24 | anchor: A02
For a curve, slow down before you enter so you need not brake in it, then gradually add speed through the curve to keep traction and control. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec08-F25 | anchor: A03
If braking in a curve cannot be avoided, press the brakes gradually until you are sure steady pressure is safe. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F26 | anchor: A03
Start steering just before the point where the road begins to bend, and stay on your own side as far right as you can. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F27 | anchor: A03
For a downhill curve, allow for gravity, shift to a lower gear before the descent, and brake earlier and slower than you would on level ground. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F28 | anchor: A03
On a right turn, keep close to the right edge so no vehicle can squeeze in between you and the curb; slow before turning and then speed up slightly. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F29 | anchor: A03
Motorcycles and bicycles are particularly hard to see while you turn, so always signal and look before turning. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F30 | anchor: A03
Following too closely is a leading cause of crashes; on the open road, leave enough space ahead that a passing vehicle could safely move into it. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F31 | anchor: A03
The two-second rule means leaving two seconds between the moment the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point and the moment you reach that point. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F32 | anchor: A03
On a highway with several lanes, check both the lane you are moving into and the lane beyond it, in case another driver is heading for the same space. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec08-F33 | anchor: A03
To change lanes, check the side and rear-view mirrors, look over your shoulder to clear the blind spot, signal ahead of time, and then move over. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0056]

Misconceptions: driving far below the limit is not automatically safe and can cause crashes; the posted limit is a ceiling, not a target, in poor conditions; oncoming drivers are allowed but not required to yield to a funeral procession; farm equipment may use most roads but not interstates; on a curve you slow before entering rather than braking in the middle of it.
Mnemonics: slow in, steady through; mirror, shoulder, signal, go; count the gap with the two-second rule.
Glossary: stopping distance means the reaction distance plus the braking distance; reaction time means the delay before you begin to brake; funeral procession means a line of vehicles escorting a funeral; blind spot means an area the mirrors do not show, cleared by a look over the shoulder.
Dynamic facts: speed limits can be changed by posted signs or by statute; the default limits here apply only where no other limit is posted.
